about.title: About Me
about.p1: I'm a Technical Instructor & Trainer specialized in the MERN stack, passionate about turning complex concepts into clear, hands-on learning experiences that actually stick. My path started in Electrical Engineering at JUST — which gave me a systems-thinking mindset I still use every day in the classroom. From there, I moved into QA Engineering, where I learned that understanding how things break is just as important as knowing how to build them.
about.p2: That combination led me naturally into teaching. Today I deliver full-stack web development training, guiding students from their first HTML tag all the way to deploying production-ready apps.
about.quote: I don't just teach syntax. I teach how to think like an engineer — how to break a problem down, read an error without panic, and build something you're genuinely proud of.

items.question: What technologies do you teach?
items.answer: I teach full-stack web development with a strong focus on the MERN stack, including React, Next.js, Node.js, Express.js, MongoDB, PostgreSQL, Firebase, and Socket.IO. I also cover Git, REST APIs, authentication, deployment, and modern frontend styling tools.

items.question: What is your teaching methodology?
items.answer: I follow a project-based learning approach. We start with a brief theoretical foundation and immediately move into live coding and building real-world projects.

items.question: How long does it take to become job-ready?
items.answer: It depends on your dedication. With my intensive roadmap, many students are ready for junior roles within 4 to 6 months of focused learning.

items.question: Is it okay to use AI tools while learning programming?
items.answer: AI tools can be helpful, but I encourage students to first build a strong understanding of programming fundamentals and problem-solving skills without depending heavily on AI. Once the basics are clear, AI can become a useful assistant for improving productivity, exploring ideas, and accelerating development workflows.

items.question: What is the most important thing you teach students?
items.answer: I always encourage students to practice consistently, build projects regularly, and never be afraid of errors. Making mistakes and debugging are essential parts of the learning process and one of the best ways to grow as a developer.
